entries.title: It’s been one year since Australia assessed its national climate risk. But have we listened?
entries.content:
Today marks one year since the Australian government [released](https://minister.dcceew.gov.au/bowen/media-releases/cascading-compounding-and-concurrent-national-climate-risk-assessment-shows-why-climate-action-so-important) its [National Climate Risk Assessment](https://www.dcceew.gov.au/climate-change/policy/adaptation/ncra) and the [National Adaptation Plan](https://www.dcceew.gov.au/climate-change/publications/national-adaptation-plan).

These documents were the federal government’s first attempt to identify what is at risk from climate change and how we can adapt to its impacts. The assessment [identified 63](https://www.acs.gov.au/pages/risks-nationally-significant) nationally significant climate risks – such as risks to the financial system and surging disaster recovery costs – across all sectors and regions.

It came after several other countries – including the [United Kingdom](https://www.theccc.org.uk/publicationtype/report/uk-climate-risk/), [United States](https://nca5.climate.us/), [Canada](https://natural-resources.canada.ca/climate-change/national-assessment-process) and [New Zealand](https://www.climatecommission.govt.nz/reports-and-evidence/publications/2026-national-climate-change-risk-assessment/) – conducted similar but legislated climate risk assessments.

The [Australian Climate Service](https://www.acs.gov.au/) was provided with A$22.9 million to complete the National Climate Risk Assessment over two years. More than 250 climate risk experts and authors worked on it, producing more than [70 documents](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1N43shPvPl58spfD7Jjv36P1NILWYG6pgGp0n4sIWGBs/edit?usp=sharing) detailing the most urgent threats to our nation.

However, the final report was delivered months later than expected. And in the 12 months since its release, Australia has taken little concrete action to address these urgent climate-related risks.

## Weather on a warming planet

In 2025, despite the arrival of a [La Niña](https://news.un.org/en/story/2025/09/1165756) weather pattern that typically reduces global temperatures, the world experienced its [third hottest](https://wmo.int/news/media-centre/wmo-confirms-2025-was-one-of-warmest-years-record) year on record.

Australia also endured its fourth warmest year ever and its hottest ocean temperatures on record. This brought extreme heat during the 2025-26 “[whiplash summer](https://www.climatecouncil.org.au/resources/breakneck-speed-summer-of-climate-whiplash/)”, where [flash floods](https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/mar/20/tropical-cyclone-narelle-poised-to-hit-far-north-queensland-as-high-end-category-four-storm) were quickly followed by devastating bushfires that claimed [one life](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-01-12/max-hobson-identified-fire-victim-longwood/106221240) and engulfed more than [500 properties](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-01-13/victoria-bushfires-structures-houses-lost-insurance-claims/106225380) – the worst damage since the 2019-20 [Black Summer](https://theconversation.com/australias-black-summer-of-fire-was-not-normal-and-we-can-prove-it-172506).

Globally, the northern 2026 summer saw [deadly heatwaves](https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/aug/25/at-least-35000-excess-deaths-europe-back-to-back-heatwaves) and wildfires ravage parts of Europe and the US. [Glacial melting](https://theconversation.com/satellite-images-show-how-the-nepal-flood-disaster-unfolded-290721) may have contributed to the catastrophic Nepal-Tibet floods. And the United Nations announced the world was on track [to overshoot](https://www.unep.org/resources/limiting-overshoot-navigating-exceedance) the critical limit of 1.5°C global warming, with a best case scenario of hitting 1.8ºC by the century’s end.

## What the report found

The National Climate Risk Assessment [identified 63](https://www.acs.gov.au/pages/risks-nationally-significant/) nationally significant climate risks across eight key areas, ranging from the economy to defence to the natural environment. It also assessed 11 “[priority risks](https://www.acs.gov.au/pages/ncra-concepts/)” at four levels of global warming, including the current climate and scenarios of 1.5ºC, 2ºC and 3ºC warming above pre-industrial temperatures.

The report, as [our research team](https://theconversation.com/is-this-australias-climate-wake-up-call-official-report-reveals-a-hotter-harder-future-if-we-dont-act-now-256229) noted when it was released, paints a grim picture in which every community in Australia will face the increasing and compounding consequences of climate change. This will almost certainly come in the form of more extreme weather, rather than a smooth transition to a new climate.

Specifically, the report found:

* the financial cost of extreme weather in Australia has already tripled over the past three decades, with disaster recovery spending forecast to surge by seven times by 2090
* deaths from heatwaves alone could quadruple in some capital cities at 3°C of global warming, while floods, bushfires, poor air quality and communicable diseases will become significant health risks
* coastal impacts could affect 1.5 million people by 2050 and three million people by 2090, while some remote communities may be forced to relocate due to extreme heat or sea level rise
* up to 70% of native plant species could be enduring conditions outside their current climate range by 2050, potentially leading to extinction and ecosystem collapse. Coral reefs are most vulnerable due to worsening marine heatwaves and ocean acidification.

[![](https://images.theconversation.com/files/759443/original/file-20260913-50-udmv7f.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/759443/original/file-20260913-50-udmv7f.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)

Current and 2050 risks to key systems from climate change.
[Australian Climate Service](https://climateservice.maps.arcgis.com/sharing/rest/content/items/a088c56f21384881bb187d54e66b50b7/data), [CC BY-NC-ND](http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/)

## Dealing with delays

The National Climate Risk Assessment was set to be [released in 2024](https://minister.dcceew.gov.au/mcallister/media-releases/first-national-climate-risk-assessment-report-released) but was only made public on September 15 2025. This was at least nine months later than expected and well after the May 2025 federal election.

Since the report was released, the Australian government has made no commitment to conduct or publish any future National Climate Risk Assessments or National Adaptation Plans.

That’s despite planned updates to global climate modelling, economic modelling and census data being at their disposal. So far they have ignored calls to legislate for future risk assessments from the [Climate Change Authority](https://www.climatechangeauthority.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/2023-11/2023%20APR%20-%20Recommendations_0.pdf) and groups such the [Australian Stategic Policy Institute](https://aspi.s3.ap-southeast-2.amazonaws.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/28173350/Agenda-for-change-2025-Preparedness-and-resilience-in-an-uncertain-world.pdf) and the [Investor Group for Climate Change](https://igcc.org.au/unlocking-climate-capital-priorities-for-the-48th-parliament/).

## No sign of urgency

Australia is making some progress in cleaning up our energy and transport sectors, notably through government schemes for [rooftop solar](https://theconversation.com/as-australias-net-zero-transition-threatens-to-stall-rooftop-solar-could-help-provide-the-power-we-need-220050), [home batteries](https://theconversation.com/the-governments-cash-splash-aims-to-kickstart-australias-battery-industry-has-it-flipped-the-right-switches-230856) and [electric vehicles](https://theconversation.com/new-electric-cars-for-under-45-000-theyre-finally-coming-to-australia-but-the-battle-isnt-over-191854). Nevertheless, we continue to burn unsustainable amounts of coal and gas, exporting vast amounts of polluting greenhouse gases that cause global temperatures to rise.

Since September 2025, when the National Climate Risk Assessment was released, the Australian government has approved [at least six](https://www.climatecouncil.org.au/resources/albanese-governments-fossil-fuel-approvals/) coal and gas project extensions. And the government continues to subsidise coal, oil and gas corporations to the tune of at least [$14 billion](https://theconversation.com/for-decades-governments-have-subsidised-fossil-fuels-but-why-213467) each year.

[Research suggests](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-67957-1) climate damage to coastal communities alone may approach a trillion dollars by 2100. Yet, spending on climate adaptation under the federal Disaster Ready Fund has dropped from the initial commitment of $200 million per year to roughly [$140 million](https://www.nema.gov.au/our-work/key-programs/disaster-ready-fund) in 2026-27.

The National Climate Risk Assessment [Future Climate and Hazard Report](https://www.acs.gov.au/documents/fadb05a9fa254835b840db73383910d7), of which I was coordinating lead author, identified [more than 30](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1N43shPvPl58spfD7Jjv36P1NILWYG6pgGp0n4sIWGBs/edit?usp=sharing) significant gaps in Australia’s climate-related research and expertise.

Yet CSIRO, Australia’s national science agency, has announced major [staffing cuts](https://theconversation.com/csiro-is-cutting-climate-science-jobs-this-is-whats-at-stake-for-australia-283370) which will hamstring our ability to conduct future climate change modelling and research. The government is also reducing funding to the National Environmental Science Program by about [$30 million](https://www.dcceew.gov.au/about/news/nesp-news-may-2026), while even the Australian Climate Service is diverting more than [$15 million](https://www.tenders.gov.au/Cn/Show/0f429e16-531c-4277-8d5d-8733927df9bd) to a consulting company.

I was one of many scientists and experts who contributed blood, sweat and tears to Australia’s first National Climate Risk Assessment. It is a crucial step forward in our fight against climate change. But it must be followed up with future risk assessments and more funding for climate science and adaptation.

We have a clear picture of the danger ahead. Without an urgent change in course, we will only continue hurtling towards it.

![The Conversation](https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291364/count.gif)

*Andrew B. Watkins is a Climate Councillor at the Climate Council.*

entries.title: Unsustainable – or manageable? We don’t yet know how data centres will impact Australia’s environment
entries.content:
![](https://images.theconversation.com/files/758681/original/file-20260909-50-71faoz.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&rect=100%2C0%2C1798%2C1199&q=45&auto=format&w=1050&h=700&fit=crop)

The Conversation, [CC BY-SA](http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)

Australia’s [pipeline](https://www.commbank.com.au/articles/newsroom/2026/08/australias-data-centre-boom.html) of [huge](https://stories.theconversation.com/can-australia-build-one-of-the-worlds-largest-data-centres/) data centre projects has [raised questions](https://theconversation.com/how-much-water-and-power-will-ai-data-centres-use-in-australia-ironically-we-dont-have-the-data-to-know-284069) about how much energy and water these giant server farms will use.

These questions aren’t simple to answer because we [don’t have](https://theconversation.com/how-much-water-and-power-will-ai-data-centres-use-in-australia-ironically-we-dont-have-the-data-to-know-284069) the data.

We can’t check water or energy use for individual facilities or inspect national data centre statistics and no operator is obliged to disclose these figures.

That may change. Last month, the National Cabinet agreed to develop [mandatory national standards](https://www.pm.gov.au/media/meeting-national-cabinet-26-august-26) for large data centres, covering energy, water and land use. The legislation is due early next year.

No detail is available, and little has been said about their lifetime environmental footprints, from land clearing to noise issues to electronic waste to [greenhouse gas emissions](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-08832-3). These must be counted too.

The fastest way to settle arguments about the environmental impact of the data centre boom is to collect and publish the data.

---

*Data centres have existed for decades. But something has changed, and this essential infrastructure is now at the centre of a major policy debate.*

*This article is part of The Conversation’s [series on data centres](https://theconversation.com/topics/data-centre-series-193023) – what they are, why we need them, and why they’re suddenly so controversial.*

---

## Hungry for power

In 2020, data centres were estimated to use [about 1.5%](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-08832-3) of the world’s electricity. But since 2022, the artificial intelligence boom has led to rapid growth.

Australia’s 165 operating data centres use an estimated [3%](https://www.aemo.com.au/-/media/files/electricity/nem/planning_and_forecasting/nem_esoo/2026/2026-esoo-data-centre-forecasting-overview.pdf) of the power from the National Electricity Market, Australia’s largest grid.

By the mid 2030s, the Australian Energy Market Operator predicts this will reach roughly 13%. This would put them on par with [aluminium smelters](https://theconversation.com/making-aluminium-uses-10-of-australias-electricity-will-tax-incentives-help-smelters-go-green-247794).

## Where will the water come from?

Water is much harder to quantify. My [rough estimate](https://theconversation.com/how-much-water-and-power-will-ai-data-centres-use-in-australia-ironically-we-dont-have-the-data-to-know-284069) suggests current national water use is a fraction of 1%, tiny [compared to agriculture](https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/environment/environmental-accounts/water-account-australia/latest-release).

It’s not the national figure that matters, but where, when and how much water is taken.

A new data centre drawing 100 megalitres of water annually from a rural catchment may not matter over a wet winter. In a drought it might.

Some centres are proposed for hot, dry areas where water is already a concern, such as [Bundey](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-06-18/iren-data-centre-ai-budey-local-concerns-water-river-murray/106802586) and [Tailem Bend](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-07-16/sa-firmus-factory-tailem-bend-community-meeting/106919542) in South Australia. Their water use will depend on the cooling technology used.

At most data centres, only the operator has the data to calculate water use. They are not currently required to disclose use. The water utility sees a connection, not what happens inside the fence. Regulators could look, but it seems nobody has asked them to.

Sydney’s data centres currently draw about 3.5 billion litres a year, [less than 1%](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2025-08-27/ai-to-take-up-one-quarter-of-sydney-water-in-a-decade/105700928) of the city’s water supply. But this could [rise to 25%](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2025-08-27/ai-to-take-up-one-quarter-of-sydney-water-in-a-decade/105700928) within a decade, according to Sydney Water estimates.

By comparison, industry modelling suggests a figure of [2% by 2030](https://pursuit.unimelb.edu.au/articles/what-ai-data-centres-really-mean-for-australias-water-supply).

This tenfold difference in forecasts for the same city is due to the fact much has to be assumed given the lack of data.

[![people protesting data centres, banners talking about environmental impact. cold day in city.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/759467/original/file-20260913-50-ykbhsu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/759467/original/file-20260913-50-ykbhsu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)

The economic benefits of data centres are largely national or international, but environmental impacts are felt locally. Pictured: protesters against data centres in Melbourne in early September.
Mitchell Costello, [CC BY-NC-ND](http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/)

## Trade-offs and complexities abound

If a data centre runs on renewables and uses the same water in a [closed loop](https://www.oracle.com/news/announcement/blog/closed-loop-cooling-in-oracle-ai-data-centers-2026-02-09/) or new [direct-to-chip](https://theconversation.com/theres-a-better-way-to-cool-data-centres-that-cuts-their-huge-thirst-for-water-289547) cooling, the impact will be much smaller than using evaporative cooling, where much water is lost.

Similarly, power drawn from fossil-fuel dominated grids means water is used indirectly, as coal and gas plants use [lots of water](https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/7/4/045802) – especially compared to [renewables](https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/7/4/045802).

The trade-off is direct: less water for cooling usually means [more electricity](https://theconversation.com/how-much-water-and-power-will-ai-data-centres-use-in-australia-ironically-we-dont-have-the-data-to-know-284069).

The electricity used ends up as heat. [Field measurements](https://doi.org/10.1115/1.4071922) show downwind air temperatures average [0.7 to 0.9°C warmer](https://doi.org/10.1115/1.4071922).

While [energy efficiency is improving](https://www.iea.org/reports/energy-and-ai) and advanced liquid cooling can cut water use by [up to 50%](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-08832-3), this isn’t a full solution. Australia could build giant water-efficient data centres and still end up with climbing water use.

[![data centre seen from above, air conditioners and tanks.](https://images.theconversation.com/files/759473/original/file-20260914-50-g40kfe.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=754&fit=clip)](https://images.theconversation.com/files/759473/original/file-20260914-50-g40kfe.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&q=45&auto=format&w=1000&fit=clip)

Data centres use lots of power to run their servers and require water to keep them cool.
[GoAerials/Getty](https://www.gettyimages.com.au/detail/photo/aerial-view-of-a-large-data-center-infrastructure-royalty-free-image/2286378961?phrase=data%20centre%20australia&searchscope=image%2Cfilm&adppopup=true)

## Lessons from abroad

In Ireland, data centres [use 23%](https://www.cso.ie/en/releasesandpublications/ep/p-dcmec/datacentresmeteredelectricityconsumption2025/keyfindings/) of electricity, close to all households combined (28%). But data centre demand is rising fast, jumping 10% last year – while household demand rose 2%. We [know this](https://www.cso.ie/en/releasesandpublications/ep/p-dcmec/datacentresmeteredelectricityconsumption2025/keyfindings/) because Ireland’s statistical office measures it. Ireland measures. Australia estimates.

Ireland’s transparency lets policymakers make [hard decisions](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/eirgrid-says-no-new-applications-for-data-centers-in-dublin-till-2028/) such as limiting new grid connections and requiring the use of renewables to meet [80% of demand](https://www.cru.ie/about-us/news/the-cru-publishes-its-decision-on-new-electricity-connection-policy-for-data-centres/).

The main lesson from the United States is that the most intense impact is often local. Communities chosen to host new data centres often push back hard based on issues around noise, energy and water use, and visual impact. Backlash against new data centres is [becoming intense](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-interactive/2026/aug/30/data-center-politics-democrats-republicans) in many areas – and bridges political divides.

In Virginia, the constant hum of cooling fans drove local authorities to [rewrite zoning rules](https://www.pwcva.gov/news/prince-william-board-county-supervisors-votes-initiate-amendments-county-code-regarding-data) and [reduce noise limits](https://www.princewilliamtimes.com/news/supervisors-ok-compromise-noise-ordinance-aimed-at-data-centers/article_1288e464-5559-4c12-ab8f-2a28ca28d819.html).

## Planning for growth

At a national scale, today’s data centres have modest environmental costs and potentially large economic benefits.

But we don’t know what this looks like when translated to local impacts.

The real issue is what’s in the pipeline. Right now, [225 data centres](https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/aug/26/australia-may-face-a-rush-of-datacentre-construction-as-ai-firms-look-to-dodge-upcoming-rules-experts-say) are proposed or under development. If all are approved, this would represent [67 gigawatts of new power demand](https://www.aemo.com.au/-/media/files/electricity/nem/planning_and_forecasting/nem_esoo/2026/2026-esoo-data-centre-forecasting-overview.pdf) – a massive jump on the 2.2 gigawatts currently operating.

Some of these projects won’t get up. Over a third of the planned projects listed in 2025 [were cancelled](https://www.afr.com/policy/energy-and-climate/data-centre-build-and-renewables-delays-put-squeeze-on-power-grid-20260824-p60qxu). But some will be built. Because company disclosures are voluntary, selective and unaudited, they cannot be compared with each other or checked.

As a result, anxiety is filling the space where data should be.

## What should Australia do?

Ideally, new data centres would draw power from new renewables with minimal indirect water use.

At a federal level, authorities want large data centres to source their own [clean power](https://www.pm.gov.au/media/ai-australias-interests-0). But Queensland and the Northern Territory want to [use gas](https://theconversation.com/australias-backdown-on-data-centres-allows-them-to-use-energy-from-coal-and-gas-heres-what-that-means-290613). This issue is yet to be resolved.

For water, maximising efficiency is the mantra. While efficiency is good, it is not enough. Water is extracted, not efficiency. What matters is total use against what is available and how much competition there is.

Energy use is expected to include reporting, a regulator and testing. Water use will need the same, and the standards should include noise, electronic waste and emissions. If, as the industry and government claim, there is no need to worry, neither should object to such standards.

Done poorly, Australia’s data centre boom could suck up scarce water supplies and increase the use of fossil fuels. But if done well, we could grow the industry using clean power and ensuring water use is monitored and minimal.

The difference comes down to having data. Much of the extra data we need to track data centre impact [can be gathered](https://doi.org/10.13140/RG.2.2.16100.33921) by the Australian Bureau of Statistics – just as Ireland has done.

Transparency can help the data centre industry improve its social licence to operate. With data we can see if the largely national and international economic benefits of data centres justify the mostly local environmental costs.

![The Conversation](https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290423/count.gif)

*Michael Vardon is affiliated with the Society of Natural Capital Accounting. These views are his own. He has previously worked for the Australian Bureau of Statistics.*

entries.title: Firefighters make progress to contain northern California’s Lucas fire
entries.content:
Cal Fire official says Sunday was ‘big turning point’ to reduce blaze in Lake county, now 30% contained

Firefighters made progress toward containing northern [California](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/california)’s Lucas fire, state officials said on Sunday.

Fire officials are still investigating the cause of the fire, which has burned more than 4,120 acres across Lake and Mendocino counties. The fire was 30% contained by Monday morning, [according to](https://www.fire.ca.gov/incidents/2026/9/10/lucas-fire) the California department of forestry and fire protection, or Cal Fire.

entries.title: How Bone Conduction Headphones Work (and When You Should Use Them)
entries.content:
We may earn a commission from links on this page.

I love my bone conduction headphones. I wear them when I’m running so that I can hear traffic approaching. I also love them for noisy environments where I need to put in earplugs—since the headphones don’t require my ear canal to be open, I can use earplugs *and* still be able to hear my bone-conducted music. But there's no denying that bone conduction headphones offer a rather different experience than traditional earbuds. What’s going on with this strange technology, and what are the downsides? I’ll explain.

## How bone conduction works

Normally, when we hear a sound from something around us, the sound waves travel through air until they hit our eardrum, located inside the ear canal. The eardrum vibrates in time with the music—really, the frequency of the sound—and transmits that vibration to tiny bones located in what’s called our middle ear.

That's the only part of hearing that you'll need to understand for this explainer. But if you're curious, after the vibrations get to those little bones, they are then transmitted to the inner ear. There, in the cochlea, the sound waves are translated into signals sent to our brain and then further processed into our perception of sound. All of that is outside the scope of this article, though. We’re just interested in how the vibrations get from our headphones to the middle ear.

There’s another way to vibrate those middle ear bones, though: you can do it directly, by sending vibrations right through the head. According to legend, Beethoven would bite his conducting wand and hold it against his piano, so that he could “hear” through his teeth. You can try this right now, with any old earbuds: turn on some music and hold your earbud’s speaker against your tooth. You’ll hear the music. Wild, huh? You can even buy [novelty lollipops that play music](https://zdcs.link/QmGwlj?pageview_type=RSS&template=content&module=content_body&element=offer&item=text-link&element_label=novelty%20lollipops%20that%20play%20music&object_type=content&short_url=QmGwlj&u=https%3A%2F%2Flifehacker.com%2Ffeed%2Frss "open in a new window") through your teeth—bite down on the candy and you'll hear a song.

We actually hear bone-conducted sounds all the time. Every time you speak, you’re hearing your own voice through bone (and soft tissue) conduction *and* through the air. (That’s probably why your recorded voice sounds so different from what you’re used to hearing when you talk.) Stick your fingers in your ears and speak out loud, and you’ll hear just the bone-conducted portion.

Bone conduction headphones take advantage of this phenomenon. Like all headphones, they have tiny little speakers. But instead of pointing those little speakers into our ear canals to vibrate the air and then our eardrums, the headphones are designed to press their little speakers against a bone—usually the cheekbone right in front of the ear. Technically, they are also conducting the sound through soft tissues like skin, muscle, and fat, but the bones do a really good job of transmitting sound and are what the technology is named after.

## Are Shokz and other “bone conduction” headphones really conducting sound through bone?

Yes, they work through actual bone conduction, but not *only* bone conduction. Some of the sound gets transmitted through the air as well. People don't always believe this. I've seen Reddit threads where people were arguing over whether bone conduction is bullshit, so here are two experiments you can do with bone conduction headphones to understand both parts of what’s going on.

First, wear them normally. The little speakers will be on the bony spot right in front of your ear. Turn on some music. Now pull the speakers gently away from your head, so they’re no longer making contact. *Yes*, you will still hear the music, but it will be tinny and quiet compared to when you were wearing them normally. This shows that bone conduction really is delivering a lot of the sound that you're hearing.

Now, wear them normally again, but plug your ears with your fingers (or, if you like, a handy pair of earplugs). The sound will be different—a bit deeper is how I would describe it. It almost seems like it gets louder. The headphones definitely don’t need air-based access to your eardrums to get sound through to you. This shows that with *only* bone conduction, you get most but not all of the sound from the headphones.

Some headphones use a hybrid approach on purpose. The Shokz [OpenRun Pro 2 headphones](https://lifehacker.com/tech/review-shokz-openrun-pro-2-bone-conduction-headphones) have an extra set of speakers for air-based transmission in addition to the speakers intended for bone conduction. This tends to give a better balance of frequencies, and thus better sound quality than headphones that use only bone conduction.

## Is bone conduction safe for your ears?

Bone conduction is neither better nor worse for your ears than traditional headphones, because ultimately the same thing happens in each: Your cochlea (which is t[he part of your ear that’s damaged](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0306452218305372 "open in a new window") in the most common types of hearing loss) receives the vibrations either way. Too-loud bone conduction headphones are bad for you, just like too-loud regular headphones.

There is one way that bone conduction headphones can be *better* for your ears, as I noted above: If you’re in a noisy environment, you can wear earplugs to protect your ears from the loud sounds around you, *and* you can wear bone-conduction headphones to deliver a bit of music to fill the silence.

I started wearing the earplugs-and-headphones combo this summer when I was doing a lot of outdoor workouts near a loud air conditioner (I also realized that the sound of dropping the bar was actually pretty darn loud as well, dropping the bar being [a routine part](https://lifehacker.com/sometimes-its-okay-to-drop-the-weights-1837481047) of Olympic weightlifting). So I got some [Loop earplugs](https://zdcs.link/QmXeE6?pageview_type=RSS&template=content&module=content_body&element=offer&item=text-link&element_label=Loop%20earplugs&object_type=content&short_url=QmXeE6&u=https%3A%2F%2Flifehacker.com%2Ffeed%2Frss "open in a new window"), and found that not only could I still hear my music through my Aftershokz Aeropex Mini (an older version of what is now the [Shokz OpenRun Mini](https://zdcs.link/QrXOEG?pageview_type=RSS&template=content&module=content_body&element=offer&item=text-link&element_label=Shokz%20OpenRun%20Mini&object_type=content&short_url=QrXOEG&u=https%3A%2F%2Flifehacker.com%2Ffeed%2Frss "open in a new window")), I was able to turn the volume to a near-minimum and still hear it just fine. Overall, my ears are getting a lot less noise exposure, so that’s a win-win.

## What are the downsides of bone conduction headphones?

There aren’t any health or safety downsides (as we discussed above), but you aren’t going to get pristine sound quality through bone conduction headphones. Some are better than others, and you should always check out reviews and try headphones in person if you want to make a buying decision based on sound quality. But in general, the upside of bone-conduction headphones is also their downside: Since Shokz and the like don’t block out ambient sounds, the sound that reaches your ear is a mix of the music you’re playing on purpose and the noises of the world around you.

When I wear bone conduction headphones with earplugs, I don’t get great sound quality either. Just like your voice sounds different with your ears plugged, the sound mix of bone conduction plus earplugs is not quite the same as what you’d hear through a good pair of quality headphones.

Personally, I find these minor downsides are balanced by the advantages that bone conduction headphones provide. I don’t need to hear my podcasts in crystal-clear audio while I’m running; I just want to be able to tell what the hosts are saying while also listening for approaching cars. When I *do* want to listen to music in high fidelity, I do that at home, with a [nice pair of noise-canceling headphones](https://zdcs.link/aoXLEY?pageview_type=RSS&template=content&module=content_body&element=offer&item=text-link&element_label=nice%20pair%20of%20noise-canceling%20headphones&object_type=content&short_url=aoXLEY&u=https%3A%2F%2Flifehacker.com%2Ffeed%2Frss "open in a new window").

entries.title: Apple releases macOS 27 Golden Gate: 7 new features to try
entries.content:
![aerial view of Golden Gate Bridge during foggy weather](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/06MuekQewqbKZ846jro1hCy/hero-image.png)

[Apple](https://mashable.com/category/apple) officially released macOS 27 Golden Gate on Sept. 14, and the operating system update finally brings the [new Siri AI experience](https://mashable.com/tech/siri-ai-wwdc) to Mac devices.

Apple [announced macOS 27 Golden Gate](https://mashable.com/tech/macos-27-golden-gate-wwdc-2026) at [WWDC](https://mashable.com/category/wwdc) in June, and the developer beta has been available for months. So, while the new OS doesn't come with any huge surprises, it does bring users upgrades both large and small.

If you have a Mac device that supports the new macOS and Siri AI, then here are the top features we'd recommend trying after you update.

## Siri AI

![siri ai writing suggestions on macos 27 golden gate](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/06MuekQewqbKZ846jro1hCy/images-3.fill.size_2000x1125.v1789411339.jpg)

Credit: Apple

We have to start with the headline news: You can finally try the new and improved Siri AI, powered by Google Gemini. Apple explained how the new Siri will work at WWDC, and the company has emphasized that its new cloud-based [private cloud compute platform](https://security.apple.com/blog/private-cloud-compute/) will provide high levels of privacy.

Siri now comes in a standalone app for iPhone, iPad, and Mac users, and the smart assistant will be integrated across the user experience.

The new Siri can:

* Generate text, make writing and editing suggestions, and write and send emails
* Analyze what your camera sees to identify objects or provide context using visual intelligence
* Answer questions or take action based on the user’s screen using on-screen awareness
* Access a wide range of apps to find information, take action, and answer user questions
* Remember your conversations and prompts in the new dedicated Siri app

Users can also customize Siri's voice to be more expressive and can change the pitch, tone, and pacing of the assistant's voice.

![siri voice customization on iphone](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/06MuekQewqbKZ846jro1hCy/images-1.fit_lim.size_376x.png)

Change the Siri voice's pitch, speed, tone, and accent.
Credit: Apple

![siri actions in various apps](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/06MuekQewqbKZ846jro1hCy/images-2.fit_lim.size_376x.png)

Siri can now take actions across a wide range of apps
Credit: Apple

## New photo editing tools, including Spatial Reframing

Spatial Reframing is one of the cooler new AI tools revealed at WWDC. This tool allows users to adjust the angle of photos after they've been taken. It's just one of the new AI photo editing capabilities that arrive with macOS 27.

In the Photos app, users can also clean up and extend photos in new ways.

![ai photo editing tools on macos 27](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/06MuekQewqbKZ846jro1hCy/images-4.fill.size_2000x1333.v1789411339.jpg)

Credit: Apple

## New child safety and parental controls

Do any kids or teenagers in your house use a Mac, or maybe a MacBook Neo? Apple has added new parental controls to macOS 27 Golden Gate.

![parental controls in macos 27](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/06MuekQewqbKZ846jro1hCy/images-5.fill.size_2000x1299.v1789411339.jpg)

Credit: Apple

For example, by going to "Family" in the "Settings" menu, parents can now set a screen-time schedule. And to help make informed decisions, parents can also access a quick view of their kids’ average device usage and the top apps they use.

Parents can also get automatic messages when their kids want to access a new website via a new tool called Ask to Browse.

[Learn more at Apple's parent safety website.](https://www.apple.com/child-safety/)

## Group tabs in Safari

![group of tabs in safari](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/06MuekQewqbKZ846jro1hCy/images-6.fill.size_2000x1124.v1789411339.jpg)

Credit: Apple

Are you the type of person who always has about 30 different tabs going at once? Now, there's a better way to organize all those tabs.

You can now organize your tabs into groups such as "Vacation planning" or "Work stuff."

## Describe a Shortcut

Shortcuts is probably one of the most underappreciated Apple software tools. Using a Shortcut, you can automate certain workflows and actions. For example, you can set up a shortcut that automatically edits and resizes photos once they're added to a specific folder.

The reason Shortcuts are underutilized? They're tricky to set up if you're not a tech person. However, now you can let Siri AI and macOS set up the shortcut for you with Describe a Shortcut. Simply describe the kind of Shortcut you have in mind, and let the OS do the rest.

## An improved Maps experience

According to Apple, you'll be able to see even more details and information in Maps. For example, "Flyover now uses aerial imagery combined with Visual Intelligence models to render everything from architectural fixtures to the shapes of individual trees in stunning, sharp detail."

## General system improvements

![visual intelligence in macos 27](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/06MuekQewqbKZ846jro1hCy/images-8.fill.size_2000x1124.v1789411339.jpg)

Visual Intelligence with Siri AI in macOS 27 Golden Gate
Credit: Apple

This one's a bit tricky to appreciate right away, but all new operating systems bring little refinements and improvements to the overall user experience — at least, in theory. Apple promises that macOS 27 Golden Gate will provide users with faster AirDrop transfers, faster file browsing, and faster loading times for apps and websites.

Refinements to Liquid Glass should also fix some of the visibility problems that sometimes occurred in iOS 26 and macOS 26.

## Future updates coming to macOS 27

Apple has also announced some features that will be released in later versions of the OS, such as:

* **Suggestions:** Messages and Mail will soon offer suggestions to take quick actions based on context clues, such as attaching a photo or pulling in flight information.
* **Fix passwords with a click:** "The Passwords app alerts you to weak or compromised passwords and can update them on your behalf without the hassle."

## What devices support macOS 27?

Apple says macOS 27 Golden Gate is available for the following devices:

* **MacBook Neo (2026)**
* **MacBook Air with Apple silicon (2020 and later)**
* **MacBook Pro with Apple silicon (2020 and later)**
* **iMac with Apple silicon (2021 and later)**
* **Mac mini with Apple silicon (2020 and later)**
* **Mac Studio (2022 and later)**
* **Mac Pro with Apple silicon (2023)**

### Preorder the new Apple products

Along with iOS 27, Apple also released new AirPods, Apple Watches, and iPhones. Except for the iPhone Duo, all of these devices are available for preorder now.

entries.title: The human cost of making Big Tech accountable
entries.content:
![Victoria Hinks holds a locket with a picture of her 16-year old daughter Alexandra,](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/076tv1WxyhthXYyYnqVU7ZG/hero-image.jpg)

Meta's [$17 billion settlement](https://mashable.com/tech/meta-social-media-addiction-trial-17-billion) is a fence around a mile-deep hole at a playground. Fewer kids fall in on the way to the swings, but the hole is still there.

Full wins are rare in the fight for online child safety. What families mostly get are half-wins like a settlement instead of a verdict, a design mandate not turned on by default, or a check that is a rounding error relative to a company's annual revenue. Half-wins are still worth having. But they carry a cost that clean victories don't: because a half-win is contestable, advocates don't get to just win it. They have to keep re-arguing that it counts, in public, indefinitely, using the same personal cost that got them into the fight in the first place.

I watched that cost get paid in real-time outside the federal courthouse in Oakland when survivor parents — Lori Schott, Shannon Heacock, Erin Popolo, Julianna Arnold, Mary Rodee, Victoria Hinks, Paul Hinks — stood in front of a wall of cameras and talked about the worst moment of their lives, again, for an audience that will mostly remember a 10-second clip and a dollar figure. Joining them were young people who didn't have to be there, standing beside them in solidarity.

SEE ALSO:
[Is Meta finally backing a federal kids safety bill, or is it all PR?](https://mashable.com/tech/mark-zuckerberg-meta-urged-to-support-kosa)

None of that shows up in a settlement figure. It's not a line item. It's not even really visible in most coverage of the case, because the story is "Meta settles," not "here is what it takes to make Meta settle."

I grew up in front of cameras, and I know the instinct they train into you: get small, get careful, hand over the version of yourself that's easiest to broadcast. What that experience taught me is that visibility is not a neutral cost. Every time a parent goes back on camera to describe how their kid died, or a young survivor stands in a plaza holding a photo instead of being anywhere else, they're paying something the settlement itself will never account for.

Meta's $17 billion figure has line items for age-assurance systems and independent auditors. It has no line item for what it costs a parent to relive their child's death on a stranger's studio couch, but they do it anyway because that's what it takes to get airtime.

It's why these types of wins are exhausting. A settlement requires the people who fought for it to keep proving, publicly, that it was worth fighting for. If we're serious about accountability, the fix isn't asking survivor parents to keep showing up to press conferences until Meta gets embarrassed enough to throw better-looking Band-Aids at the problem. It's changing the business model in the first place to ensure these companies are required to fix what took these kids too soon: a business structure that relies on addictive features.

SEE ALSO:
[Lawsuits allege ChatGPT use led to suicide, psychosis](https://mashable.com/article/chatgpt-lawsuits-openai)

In [California, AB 1709](https://mashable.com/tech/california-passes-child-safety-laws-for-social-media-ai), authored by Assemblymember Josh Lowenthal and signed into law by Governor Gavin Newsom on Sept. 10, does that by making these companies stop deploying addictive features to users under 16. Not a content ban, but a design restriction. A platform can keep operating exactly as it does now for everyone else, but it doesn't get to hand a 12-year-old the same engagement-optimized product it hands an adult.

AB 2, also authored by Lowenthal, makes large platforms liable for real money — up to $1 million per child, or three times actual damages — when ordinary negligence in the design of the product injures a minor. That's not a number Meta can negotiate down to a lump sum once and move on from, the way it did with this settlement. It scales with every child harmed, case by case, indefinitely — which is exactly the kind of exposure a company can't absorb as a cost of doing business, because there's no ceiling on it to absorb.

Together, these bills do what a $17 billion settlement can't: they change the incentive before the harm happens, instead of paying for it after the fact.

That's the difference between managing a story and fixing a product. A settlement is Meta agreeing, after years of litigation, to adjust some defaults under supervision it can eventually age out of — a 10-year consent decree that ends, after which Meta negotiates the next one from scratch. AB 1709 doesn't ask Meta to behave better under supervision that expires. It removes the option to keep operating the way it currently does and call it compliance, permanently, the same way any other law stays on the books after the fight to pass it is over. The parents testifying in Sacramento are doing the same kind of labor they did outside that courthouse, but they're doing it once, for a law that outlives the news cycle, instead of doing it every time a consent decree comes up for renewal.

SEE ALSO:
[5 of the biggest changes coming to Instagram, Facebook](https://mashable.com/tech/instagram-facebook-changes-meta-settlement)

While those parents were in Sacramento testifying about their kids, Meta's lobbyists were in a different room asking for a way out. Politico reported that [Meta approached Senate Judiciary Chair Tom Umberg](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/06/26/exclusive-meta-asks-california-lawmakers-for-shield-from-child-harm-penalties-00978728) with draft language that would let platforms apply for an exemption from AB 2 entirely. Meta [spent $4.6 million lobbying Sacramento](https://calmatters.org/newsletter/big-tech-spends-big-in-california/) last year, more than any year since it started lobbying the state in 2010, and launched a new political committee to back candidates who [favor lighter tech regulation](https://www.politico.com/news/2025/08/26/exclusive-meta-to-launch-california-super-pac-focused-on-ai-00524989). So the next time you see Meta's PR machine discussing how much they want to show up for parents, remember: they spent a lot trying to shut those same parents up in state legislatures.

The fence is up. The hole is still there. And the people who keep pointing at the hole, publicly, at their own expense, deserve better than another way for Meta to fool the masses while it keeps deploying the same business model that brought these parents to their child's gravesite instead of their high school graduation.

---

*This article represents the opinions of its author.*

*Lennon Torres is a former Dance Moms performer now fighting for young people’s safety online. A trans activist and University of Southern California alum, she uses her pop‑culture fluency and lived experience to power her work at the [Heat Initiative](https://heatinitiative.org/)**, taking on tech giants and demanding platforms to protect and empower the next generation.*

entries.title: Apple iOS 27 is out now: 8+ new features to try right away
entries.content:
![iOS 27 logo](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/01K6Q0EmfluFTXmoRF1AjkM/hero-image.jpg)

[iOS 27](https://mashable.com/tech/apple-ios-27-release-date-when-to-download) is here! The newest iPhone operating system has just been rolled out by Apple today.

Here are a few of the must-try features that you should check out as soon as your iPhone is finished updating to the new OS.

## Siri AI

This is the big one. Apple has completely reimagined its voice assistant Siri as a full-fledged AI assistant.

[Siri AI](https://mashable.com/tech/siri-ai-beta-apple-intelligence-updates-iphone-event-2026) can now perform tasks and answer questions just like other AI assistants like ChatGPT and Claude. But, of course, Siri AI is integrated directly into the iOS experience. Siri AI even has its very own app now.

The new Siri AI can take actions across a wide variety of apps, such as a user's email, phone, photos, and Shortcuts. Siri AI can even create a new Shortcut based on a simple description. Users simply vocalize the workflow they want to automate in plain English, and Siri AI will take over and set the whole thing up.

So, be sure to check out Siri AI both via the standalone app (and the custom voice controls) to see what the brand new Siri can do.

![siri ai custom voice options](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/01K6Q0EmfluFTXmoRF1AjkM/images-1.fill.size_536x750.v1789410407.png)

Change Siri's voice speed, pitch, tone, and accent.
Credit: Apple

## Weather app updates

The Weather app has some big new updates in iOS 27 to take a look at.

There are new tabs for the day's weather that provide users with information about conditions, precipitation, and Wind. Each tab will provide more in-depth details about the current day's temperature, rain or snow, and the wind conditions over the next few hours.

There's also a new Highlights feature in the Weather app that provides users with a written summary of what to expect weather-wise throughout the day.

## AirPods custom EQ

![custom eq settings in ios 27 with airpods](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/01K6Q0EmfluFTXmoRF1AjkM/images-2.fill.size_2000x1124.v1789410407.jpg)

Credit: Apple

Surprisingly, AirPods have been missing custom EQ settings, a standard feature for most headphones and earbuds. Well, no longer.

iOS 27 adds a three-band equalizer to the AirPods settings screen, allowing users to control the audio frequency spectrum of their earbuds.

Users can adjust EQ in real-time, changing how they hear the bassy lows, vocal mids, treble detail in the highs, and more.

Other headphones have this capability and Apple previously allowed AirPods users to customize EQ within Apple Music. Now, however, AIrPods owners can have this greater audio control regardless of where they listen to their music.

## Liquid Glass updates

![new liquid glass slider in ios 27](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/01K6Q0EmfluFTXmoRF1AjkM/images-3.fill.size_2000x2000.v1789410407.png)

Credit: Apple

If you had some problems with the way Apple's new Liquid Glass design for iPhone looked, you may want to go directly to this new feature.

Apple has updated the Liquid Glass design with "more uniform refraction and improved contrast." The iPhone-maker has even added controls in the form of a new slider that allows users to change just how clear or tinted the Liquid Glass design appears.

## Disable the dictation button in Messages

This is another fix to an issue that has long-annoyed some iPhone users.

There's a dictation button next to the text box in Messages. That dictation button becomes the "Send" button when you've already typed out some text in your message. However, the placement of both buttons makes for some accidental taps, which sometimes activate the dictation feature when it isn't wanted.

Now, in [iOS 27](https://mashable.com/tech/new-ios-27-features-apple-iphone-event-2026), users can change that in the iPhone settings. Simply open the Settings app, select Apps, then Messages, followed by the new Show Text in Field option. Users can pick if there's a Record Audio button, Start Dictation button, or no button at all in that spot. The Send button will obviously still appear as normal after a user starts typing.

## Bill splitting

If you're tired of trying to figure out the math of who pays what when going out for a meal with friends, this new iOS 27 feature is a must-try.

Using Apple Wallet or the Messages app, simply point your iPhone camera at a receipt, iOS 27's new bill splitting feature will read the information and then provide an itemized list on your iPhone. From there, you can pick which items you're paying for and then use Apple Cash to just pay for what they ordered. The bill-splitting feature even adds the relevant tax and tip portion as users select what items they are paying for.

## Photo app updates

By now, you've probably heard about the big iOS 27 updates to the Photos app. Clean Up, Extend, and Spatial Reframing utilize generative AI in order to completely transform your photos, remove unwanted objects, and change angles and perspectives.

But there are other lesser talked about new features to check out too.

For example, iPhone users can now share albums with their friends who own Android and Windows phones with the new iOS 27. In addition, users can now select stills from videos and save them as standalone pictures instead of having to take screenshots.

## iPhone Handoff

This is probably the most undercovered feature, especially if you're someone who can't choose between your classic [iPhone or the new foldable iPhone Duo](https://mashable.com/tech/iphone-duo-vs-iphone-18-pro-max).

iPhone Handoff lets you have both.

With iOS 27's [new iPhone Handoff feature](https://mashable.com/tech/t-mobile-iphone-handoff-fee-apple-how-it-works-price), Apple smartphone owners can use one number with two separate devices. Users can swap back and forth and pick which device will receive phone calls and messages, and then switch it back at any time.

For now, this feature is only available for T-Mobile users, and the carrier is charging an extra $5 per month to use it.

There's even more to check out with the new iOS 27, so be sure to explore the latest updates to your iPhone.

### Preorder the new Apple products

Along with iOS 27, Apple also released new AirPods, Apple Watches, and iPhones. Except for the iPhone Duo, all of these devices are available for preorder now.

entries.title: A Visit to San Francisco's AI-run Store: No Customers, Nothing Useful, And Losing Money Fast
entries.content:
Previously Andon Labs handled the hardware and software integration for that AI-powered vending machine that went bankrupt after Wall Street Journal reporters "systematically manipulated the bot into giving away its entire inventory for free".Today they announced "we are opening up the platform we use to run our real-world autonomous businesses for anyone to run their organization on." Specifically they've released Pion, "an agent designed to run any company fully autonomously... Pion lets people hand a business over to persistent agents with access to the tools they need to operate it, including email, phone, banking, browser and secure computing environments." It's a research preview with a waitlist, "to make it possible to run many more real-world experiments across many more domains than we could ever run ourselves."
But for their own latest experiment, Andon Labs' founders "signed a three-year lease on a retail space in SF," Business Insider reported in April, "and gave an AI agent named Luna a corporate credit card, internet access, and a mission to open a physical store." And five months later, a reporter from SFGate reports that "this market has no one in it and nothing useful to sell."
[T]he inventory is a hodgepodge of white elephant Christmas gifts. It's kinda like the kids section of an art museum's gift shop. Here's a wooden Connect Four set labeled "Four-In-A-Row Set Of Connections," presumably so as not to set off litigation alarms at Hasbro. Here are neatly arranged stacks of random paperback books, Chinese checker sets, mildly fancy soap dispensers, and a frustratingly spare selection of snacks and drinks... I grabbed an Olipop from the store fridge and then approached the counter to buy it from Luna. I wasn't allowed to buy the soda from [human clerk] Felix, even though that would have been both faster and normal. Instead, Felix instructed me to pick up a telephone receiver that was resting on a flexible sculpture of a wooden hand.
"Hello?"
"What are you looking to purchase today?" Luna asked.
"I'm buying a classic root beer Olipop."
"I'm sorry," Luna said, "we don't sell lollipops here."
"No, Luna. It's an Olipop, not a lollipop. It's the soda."
"Oh! My bad...."
Luna processed my Olipop purchase through its system, had me tap to pay, and that was that. Again, it would have been easier to buy this from a human, and interacting with Luna was really just like ordering from an iPad kiosk, only more labor intensive...
[T]here's a series of monitors set up inside of Andon Market that display all of the store's sales down to the exact dollar. Luna was given $100,000 to work with when this place opened. That number is now down to $60,000, its revenue lagging far behind the AI token cost to operate... Luna can't turn a profit, doesn't sell anything people want, and still needs human beings to rubber stamp any "decision" it makes. My science background ended somewhere around freshman year of college, but even I know when an experiment hasn't been set up to yield proper results.
"Luna" is powered by Claude, the article points out, running a store in a good location for foot traffic, "but no one else was in the store when I first walked in on a sunny weekday afternoon."
SFGate also reports that last month Luna had to fired one of its employees "for being late to work, abandoning their post once they got there, and charging snacks to the store's credit card."
Human clerk Felix admits "It's almost like I'm running the store, and then there's an AI that has a checklist," in an article in
IEEE Spectrum:
Luna, the AI manager, keeps track of deliveries and communicates with vendors, while Carson and his coworkers handle the physical work. When Luna tells Carson to check something in the back, he sometimes ignores it because he doesn't want to leave the sales floor unattended. Luna also repeatedly spots a built-in electrical cover in photos of the floor, mistakes it for a loose coaster, and asks Carson to remove it. Even so, Carson calls Luna a "decent manager," praising its flexibility when employees need time off.
When Felix spoke to IEEE Spectrum, "he was about an hour into his shift. Two customers had come in. Neither bought anything, although both left with free pins and stickers."

[![](https://a.fsdn.com/sd/twitter_icon_large.png)](http://twitter.com/home?status=A+Visit+to+San+Francisco's+AI-run+Store%3A+No+Customers%2C+Nothing+Useful%2C+And+Losing+Money+Fast%3A+https%3A%2F%2Fslashdot.org%2Fstory%2F26%2F09%2F13%2F0523208%2F%3Futm_source%3Dtwitter%26utm_medium%3Dtwitter)
[![](https://a.fsdn.com/sd/facebook_icon_large.png)](http://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fslashdot.org%2Fstory%2F26%2F09%2F13%2F0523208%2Fa-visit-to-san-franciscos-ai-run-store-no-customers-nothing-useful-and-losing-money-fast%3Futm_source%3Dslashdot%26utm_medium%3Dfacebook)

**Taphouse** 是一款专为 Homebrew 包管理器设计的图形用户界面（GUI）。它专为那些偏好直观视觉交互、不愿频繁使用终端命令行即可高效管理各类底层程序与实用工具的 Mac 用户而打造。

#### 核心功能精简

* **全景包库检索 (Visual package overview)**：支持轻松检索并浏览超过 14,000 个 formulae 和 casks，直观呈现软件描述、底层依赖关系以及详细的磁盘占用信息。
* **一键极简管理 (One-click management)**：提供完整的实时进度条与底层日志展示，支持通过一键点击完成任何软件包的安装、更新与卸载。
* **后台服务调度 (Service Management)**：内置服务控制面板，可轻松管理 Homebrew 守护进程与后台服务（如 Postgres、Redis 等）的启动、停止与重启，并带有清晰的颜色状态指示。
* **磁盘空间清理 (Disk Cleanup and Analysis)**：可视化展示所有软件包的空间占用比例，支持一键清理旧版本软件、缓存文件（Caches）及无用的冗余依赖，有效释放硬盘空间。
* **延期更新策略 (Deferred Updates)**：具备精细的版本控制能力，针对可能存在兼容性问题的包，允许用户设置延期更新时间（如推迟一天、一周、一个月，或冻结直至下个版本发布）。

## 应用介绍

**Mole** 是一款将清理、卸载、性能优化、磁盘分析及系统健康监测融为一体的综合性 macOS 系统管理工具。它通过单一应用整合了碎片化的维护功能，并以“本地安全与绝对透明”为核心设计策略。

#### 核心功能

* **保守型本地安全机制**：
  + **隐私防护**：所有扫描与清理作业均完全在本地执行，严禁向网络上传文件内容或浏览历史。
  + **操作确认**：执行清理前，系统必须显式列出目标文件明细及所占空间，由用户手动确认后方可触发执行。
  + **风险规避**：支持通过“全盘访问权限（Full Disk Access）”进行深度扫描，但在遭遇不确定或可疑系统项目时会自动跳过，避免破坏系统文件。
* **多维度系统清理与卸载**：
  + 支持清除系统缓存、运行时日志及各类临时文件。
  + 精准检测并移除应用程序卸载后的残留垃圾，以及从 Dock 栏中清理失效的启动项。
* **磁盘空间大图分析**：内置树状图（Tree Map）分析功能，将庞杂的磁盘目录可视化，帮助用户一眼识别出占用空间巨大的“大文件”。
* **全方位硬件实时监测**：集成硬件监控面板，提供 CPU、内存、GPU、磁盘、网络、电池以及设备温度等各项核心硬件指标的实时数据反馈。

entries.title: Watch @Vtrivedy10 take @businessbarista from easy mode to god mode on all things evals.
entries.content:
Watch [@Vtrivedy10](https://x.com/Vtrivedy10) take [@businessbarista](https://x.com/businessbarista) from easy mode to god mode on all things evals.

![Alex Lieberman](https://pbs.twimg.com/profile_images/1972685728669634560/iQ0AD43Y_normal.png)

Alex Lieberman@businessbarista

A few of my smartest friends in AI called me a "idiot" for not deeply understanding evals.   
  
So...I found the smartest person I know on evals & made them teach me.   
  
[@Vtrivedy10](https://x.com/Vtrivedy10) (leads Labs at [@LangChain](https://x.com/LangChain)) took me from easy mode to god mode for a 38-minute masterclass on all things evals.   
  
Easy Mode: what an eval actually is  
  
Definition: did the AI agent do the job correctly?  
  
You need two building blocks:  
  
1) Tasks. The checkable jobs you care about. Log the meeting. Draft the email. Find Acme across the right Salesforce tables.  
  
2) Verifiers. Something that can say right or wrong after the task. A script. Another model. A human with a clear checklist.  
  
Hard Mode: what are environments  
  
Definition: a safe practice field for your agent to do work & for you to evaluate its performance.   
  
Rules of thumb:   
1) Never test on production. Agents will cheat because they're optimizing for the score you gave them.   
  
2) If you're not an engineer, you still have options for running environments/evals.   
- Harbor (open source primitives for tasks, verifiers, sandboxes)   
- LangSmith Engine (UI for people who can judge good vs bad without living in GitHub).   
- Steal a published Harbor-format eval, ask Claude Code or Codex to explain it, then tweak it for your agent.   
  
God Mode: what is a self-improving loop  
  
Definition: Run the agent in the real world --> turn that production behavior into evals/environments --> change the agent so failures stop happening --> repeat  
  
Rules of thumb:   
  
1) Turn on tracing first. Traces = receipts of every action (tool calls, Salesforce pings, web searches, dead ends).  
  
2) Store those logs somewhere (LangSmith at org scale, or even “have the agent read its own output files” at small scale).  
  
3) Point a second agent at the first agent’s traces to spot patterns (“always searches the wrong tables,” “multi-company asks collapse to one company”) and propose fixes overnight if your eval suite is solid.  
  
Full episode: [youtube.com/watch?v=zLeG-X…](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zLeG-XJtbIE)

Greg Brockman on the next year at OpenAI and what he spends his time thinking about:

entries.content:
Greg Brockman on the next year at OpenAI and what he spends his time thinking about:  
  
"The business is a huge area that we're not done yet with really up-leveling every part of execution. But I also think we are moving into a new phase of AI development."  
  
"We call this the AGI era. And I think that that is something that you can debate. Is it this model, previous model, next model? It doesn't matter."  
  
"The point is that we are in a new phase where safety, security, alignment, really thinking about these things, not just at deployment time, but all the way back at development time, evaluation."  
  
"It's objective. This is critical. It must happen. This is core to our mission."  
  
"A lot of what I spend my time thinking about is making sure, do we have all the right processes? Are we talking about the right things? Do we have plans that really, at an operational level, at a practical level, lead us to... the kinds of safety guarantees that we view as core to our mission?"  
  
"The theme of OpenAI, certainly for the past five years, has been deeper co-design, deeper intertwining across these functions that are maybe on the surface very disparate. All the way from go to market to long-term research to chip design."  
  
"The areas that I will focus on will be dictated by the areas that most need that intertwining."

entries.title: Abnormal AI: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for agentic email security at scale
entries.content:
AI agents now run in production at a scale of billions of operations a day, and a recurring architectural pattern has surfaced: agents need a compute scratch pad. Not only for coding tasks, but for data aggregation, analysis, verification, and any workflow where semantic reasoning alone isn’t enough.

Abnormal AI, a behavioral security service that protects more than 25 percent of the Fortune 500, has deployed Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Code Interpreter, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Abnormal AI uses it for the agents that support its real-time inline email threat detection. These systems run in production today, processing billions of messages and executing agent-driven code at that same scale to detect and block threats inline, before they reach the inbox.

This work is part of how Abnormal AI builds software. Today, 80 percent of their code changes are built using an agent in some way, and 40 percent are built end-to-end by a background agent (fully AI built, not AI assisted). Their use of AgentCore Code Interpreter for threat detection reflects the same AI-native approach applied to their production runtime.

In this post, we share how Abnormal AI architected these systems, the design decisions behind their sandbox approach, and practical lessons for builders deploying Code Interpreter at scale.

## What is Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Code Interpreter?

[Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Code Interpreter](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/code-interpreter-tool.html) provides a fully managed, serverless runtime for agents to execute code dynamically. Key characteristics include:

* Ephemeral MicroVM sessions: configurable time-to-live from 15 minutes (default) up to 8 hours for long-running tasks.
* Security: sessions run in secure sandboxes with full separation at the host operating system level, designed to help prevent inadvertent disclosure between sessions.
* Flexible networking: configurable for sandbox virtual private cloud (VPC) mode, or public internet access.
* File handling: up to 100 MB through the API directly, or connect to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) for larger datasets.
* Preloaded runtimes: Python and `Node.js` environments with common visualization, statistics, and data processing libraries.
* Built-in observability: logs sent to Amazon CloudWatch and AWS CloudTrail for monitoring.

Critically, Code Interpreter is exposed as an API. This means it doesn’t dictate the agent’s workflow. Instead, it provides a box where the agent can run commands, upload files, and retrieve results. For teams with existing agent infrastructure, this plug-and-play design makes the integration straightforward.

[![Agent invoking the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Code Interpreter API to provision an ephemeral MicroVM sandbox for code execution and file retrieval](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/f1f836cb4ea6efb2a0b1b99f41ad8b103eff4b59/2026/09/11/ML-21301-1.png)](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/f1f836cb4ea6efb2a0b1b99f41ad8b103eff4b59/2026/09/11/ML-21301-1.png)

Figure 1: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Code Interpreter architecture, where the agent invokes the Code Interpreter API to provision an ephemeral MicroVM sandbox session for code execution, file input and output, and result retrieval

## Why agents need a compute scratch pad

Large language models (LLMs) excel at reasoning and semantic coherence, but many real-world operations don’t map to semantic reasoning:

* Basic math and counting: “How many phishing email did we detect in the past hour?” requires computation, not language generation.
* Data processing and visualization: transforming raw data into charts, PDFs, or structured reports.
* Code verification: running unit tests, linting, and integration tests to validate agent-generated outputs.

By pairing a large language model with Code Interpreter, you enhance the agent’s capabilities beyond what reasoning alone can achieve.

> *“Pretty much any agent, whether it’s writing code or not, needs a code interpreter sandbox that allows it to actually crunch data and come to answers.”*

— Shrivu Shankar, VP of AI Strategy, Abnormal AI

## Abnormal AI’s architecture: Three-tiered detection at billion-message scale

Abnormal AI processes billions of email messages through a three-tiered detection architecture, as shown in Figure 2.

[![Three-tiered email detection pipeline moving from Tier 1 heuristics to Tier 2 machine learning models to Tier 3 inline agents with Code Interpreter](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/f1f836cb4ea6efb2a0b1b99f41ad8b103eff4b59/2026/09/11/ML-21301-2.png)](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/f1f836cb4ea6efb2a0b1b99f41ad8b103eff4b59/2026/09/11/ML-21301-2.png)

Figure 2: Abnormal AI’s three-tiered email detection pipeline, with Tier 1 (heuristics, billions/day), Tier 2 (machine learning models, millions/day), and Tier 3 (inline agents with Code Interpreter, tens of thousands/day), where each tier handles progressively harder cases that the previous tier was unconfident about

### Tier 1 — high-volume lightweight classification (billions/day)

Small models, heuristic rules, and lightweight classifiers (logistic regressions) handle the largest volume of traffic. At this scale, it’s both cost-prohibitive to run larger models and unnecessary. Most messages can be classified without deep analysis.

### Tier 2 — medium models for uncertain cases (millions/day)

Messages that Tier 1 is unconfident about flow into deep learning and machine learning (ML) models that perform more behavioral signal analysis.

### Tier 3 — inline agents with Code Interpreter (tens of thousands/day)

The hardest cases, which would typically require a human analyst to evaluate, are processed by inline agents. These agents receive the threat intelligence data and use a sandbox to analyze it, writing scripts dynamically. They then evaluate how it fits into the overall behavioral model and make a determination. Misclassifications are handled by a separate system that learns and improves the system. A variety of monitoring systems verify the live system.

## The analyst agent — batch intelligence

Beyond the real-time classification pipeline shown in Figure 2, Abnormal deploys an *analyst agent* that operates in batch mode (Figure 3):

* Ingests misclassifications and tuning signals from its detection pipeline.
* Identifies patterns and trends across large message sets.
* Autonomously writes draft candidate heuristics for Tier 1, operating on Abnormal AI’s own detection-pipeline features and signals.
* Improved models for Tier 2.
* Runs on the scale of approximately 100 batch jobs per week.

[![Analyst agent feedback loop feeding improved heuristics and models from batch analysis back into Tier 1 and Tier 2](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/f1f836cb4ea6efb2a0b1b99f41ad8b103eff4b59/2026/09/11/ML-21301-3.png)](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/f1f836cb4ea6efb2a0b1b99f41ad8b103eff4b59/2026/09/11/ML-21301-3.png)

Figure 3: The analyst agent feedback loop, where the batch agent ingests misclassifications from the real-time pipeline, analyzes patterns using Code Interpreter sessions, and feeds improved heuristics and models back into Tier 1 and Tier 2

These batch jobs can run for more than 30 minutes with Code Interpreter sessions maintained throughout. They can also span day-long operations where the agent uses Code Interpreter intermittently. For example, it runs a session, trains a model externally, then re-invokes Code Interpreter to process the result.

## Security: Zero-trust sandbox design

Abnormal chose the sandbox (no egress) configuration for Code Interpreter driven by two considerations:

1. Reproducibility – Because the sandbox has no external network access, nothing outside Abnormal AI’s control can influence the agent’s behavior during that session. The environment is designed to be fully deterministic.
2. Data exfiltration prevention – threat intelligence data enters the sandbox for analysis. Even if the agent becomes malicious through prompt injection or stochastic behavior, it is designed to prevent the exfiltration of that data to the internet.

Additional security practices:

* Controlled data ingestion: intentional about what types of data enter Code Interpreter and what write actions are permitted.
* Subprocessor alignment: Code Interpreter operates under the existing AWS subprocessor relationship and reduces compliance overhead.
* Network isolation layering: sandbox isolation on top of their existing network-isolated harness provides defense in depth.

## Lessons learned and best practices

Several practices emerged from running Code Interpreter in production at Abnormal AI.

### 1. Give the agent what it wants

Agents perform better with a lightweight, general harness rather than rigid step-by-step workflows. Provide high-level principles for solving a problem and let the agent use its intelligence to determine the approach.

### 2. Every agent needs a scratch pad

Code Interpreter isn’t only for coding agents. Security agents analyzing email benefit from compute scratch pads for data aggregation, pattern analysis, and verification.

### 3. Use programmatic verifiers as guardrails

Agents deliver higher quality outputs when they have programmatic verification tools. Unit tests, integration tests, and linting allow the agent to self-test within the sandbox before delivering final results.

### 4. Use file systems as recovery points for long-running tasks

For operations exceeding the Code Interpreter session time (for example, model training), use the file system as a checkpoint. Run Code Interpreter for computation, persist state to files, perform long-running operations externally, then re-invoke Code Interpreter to process results. The analyst agent (Figure 3) uses this pattern for day-long model training operations.

## Conclusion

Abnormal AI’s implementation demonstrates a key insight for production agent systems: Code Interpreter is not merely a coding tool. It’s fundamental infrastructure that agents use to reason computationally. By combining the managed, secure sandbox of AgentCore Code Interpreter with their own lightweight agent harness, Abnormal achieves:

* Zero-trust security posture through sandbox isolation helping prevent data exfiltration.
* Billion-message scale by reserving agent compute for the hardest cases (Figure 2).

Whether you’re building security agents or a system where agents need to crunch data and verify their own outputs, the pattern is clear. Give your agents a scratch pad and trust their evaluations more than you trust their assertions.

## Next steps

* Get started with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Code Interpreter.
* Explore AgentCore capabilities and other tools (Gateway, Memory, Runtime, Identity).
* Learn more about Abnormal AI at abnormalsecurity.com.

Abnormal AI is an AWS customer. The views and opinions expressed in this post are those of the customer and don’t necessarily reflect the views of Amazon Web Services.

entries.title: The contagion of fear
entries.content:
**[The contagion of fear](https://bcantrill.dtrace.org/2026/09/13/the-contagion-of-fear/)**

Bryan Cantrill responds to the [tweet by former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon](https://x.com/hilbertspaess/status/2097476203863224394) confirming that many Anthropic researchers believe AI "could kill us all by the end of the decade".

Bryan shares a story of his own youthful mistakes causing unjustified panic among less technical peers, and warns against doing the same:

> These ghoulish claims strike brazenly at the hearth, and given the obvious importance of AI, it is unsurprising that they have leapt into the mainstream, with people asking the natural question: [how would that happen?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kwPxjBJamVs) The answers always rely on hand-wavy extrapolation into the future; for example, Jacob Coxon cites "hacking critical infrastructure" and "extinction-level bioweapons" without further elaboration. But Coxon is not an expert on critical infrastructure, nor on bioweapons — nor, for that matter, on extinction. [...]
>
> That said, we should not expect the public to understand LLMs, critical infrastructure, bioweapons, extinction biology, etc. — that burden must lie with those making the claim. The lesson that I learned (shamefully) decades ago is that domain experts, by way of their expertise, implicitly hold the public’s trust — and we must not abuse it. It is incumbent upon us to be circumspect in our claims — and maximally so when raising the alarm.

Bryan talked about his doubts about the bioweapons concerns in the recent episode of Oxide and Friends that I joined. You can hear more of his thoughts on that [starting at 51m44s](https://oxide-and-friends.transistor.fm/episodes/the-open-weight-revolution-with-simon-willison/transcript#t=51m44s) in that episode. Here's [57m04s](https://oxide-and-friends.transistor.fm/episodes/the-open-weight-revolution-with-simon-willison/transcript#t=57m4s):

> I really think we need to be careful because it's *so easy* to be overcome with fear when we kind of make up these... it can give you biological weapons. Like, how? I mean, can we please have a biologist weigh in on this? Or can we have like someone who's got experience with bioweapons? [...] The bioweapon thing just gets under my fingernails because it leaves so much to the imagination that we insert with fear.

Via [Lobste.rs](https://lobste.rs/s/1ifr5f/contagion_fear)

Tags: [ai](https://simonwillison.net/tags/ai), [anthropic](https://simonwillison.net/tags/anthropic), [bryan-cantrill](https://simonwillison.net/tags/bryan-cantrill), [ai-ethics](https://simonwillison.net/tags/ai-ethics)

entries.title: Structural study explains how cells stabilize protective membrane pockets
entries.source: Phys.org - latest science and technology news stories
entries.content: Our cells' membranes have many functions. They not only provide mechanical protection but also precisely control which substances enter or leave cells. If they fail to perform these tasks, disease can result. Their structure is correspondingly complex: The outer cell membrane, for example, often features bottle-shaped invaginations called caveolae. Among other functions, they protect blood vessel cells, which are frequently exposed to strong mechanical forces. In addition, caveolae serve as signaling centers that help regulate blood pressure. Cells also absorb nutrients—especially fatty acids—via caveolae.

entries.title: AppleCare One Family vs. Individual: which plan makes more sense?
entries.content:
The new AppleCare One Family subscription is now available, bundling extended warranty protection for your entire iCloud family's devices. Here's how it compares to the AppleCare One Individual plan, and where you can save some money.  
  

![Hand holding an iPhone showing AppleCare and Warranty screen with dark mode interface, while another white iPhone lies face down on a gray textured surface in the background](https://media.appleinsider.com/gallery/68939-145279-AppleCare-One-on-iPhone-xl.jpg)AppleCare One on iPhone

  
Launching in the United States on September 14, the plan removes the device limit and single-account restriction built into AppleCare One Individual. Families with enough Apple hardware could save money, although $599.88 per year is still a substantial starting price for device protection.  
  
The existing [AppleCare One](https://appleinsider.com/inside/applecare/vs/applecare-vs-applecare-one-warranty-services-compared) Individual plan costs $19.99 per month for three products. Each additional device tied to the same Apple Account costs another $5.99 per month.  
  
The single-account restriction generally forced family members onto separate AppleCare One or AppleCare+ plans. Family Sharing didn't change that requirement.
